sentences.gloss_en: Welcome to a new explainer.
Today we dive into the world of data and specifically take apart the architecture of the Huawei DataCube platform.
We'll see how this platform takes raw operational data, the raw and very messy operating data, and works magic on it.
So it turns it into business intelligence and a very clear view, specifically for mobile money services.
The subject really is like brilliant engineering.
Our journey today is fast and exciting.
We'll walk with the data from the moment it enters the system until it comes out as a report.
We'll pass through five stations: architecture, the star schema, our kitchen the ETL, then the Daily Report, and we'll serve it with Governance and Masking.
Let's get straight into it and start with the first station, architecture and storage.
How do we build the foundation that will carry all of this?
Imagine with me how we could take more than 50 raw data sources and turn them into a clear business view.
The challenge here is not only the count; the challenge is the speeds.
We pull data from the Mobile Money platform every 15 minutes, from billing every hour, and from CRM once a day.
Chaos, right? Every source has its own rhythm, and that represents a huge challenge.
The solution starts from here.
DataCube is not just a separate dashboard we look at and that's it; it's a complete architecture running as a connected pipeline.
It starts from the sources, then passes through the ETL layer for merging and cleaning.
Then it enters the storage layers to be stored, and finally reaches the analytics and reporting layer.
Step by step, this chaos turns into a precise system.
The table shows its division very cleverly: we have three storage layers.
First the ODS, which is for raw data with retention of just days, and it is used by the ETL developers.
Second the DW, or Data Warehouse, which keeps a full history for years and is used by the analysts.
Finally the Data Mart, which offers ready summaries for specific departments, with history in months, aimed more at business managers.
Each one has its own use.
And no single storage fits everything, right?
This decision tree shows what we use and when.
If we need an instant response, HBase and Redis are the solution.
For very large data that needs batch processing, we go to Hive.
For historical analysis and complex joins, we use GaussDB.
And raw data lands as it is on HDFS.
Each technology is placed in its right place; the data is stored and has become safe.
Let's move on to the Star Schema and Matrix stage and see how we organize these numbers so the business can understand them and benefit from them.
The most important rule here, which we call the grain, confirms a fundamental principle.
This rule is the foundation on which the Mobile Money star schema is built, and all the facts and dimensions that come after.
If this foundation is sound, everything after it will be sound.
Based on this foundation, we can produce 24 measures, or 24 KPIs.
So these numbers stay manageable, we divide them into five main families, and finally the system's own indicators.
This division makes the huge numbers very easy to digest.
To understand this practically, look at this number: 33.33 dollars.
It's not a random number; it's a calculated average.
Imagine we have 15 thousand transactions with a total value of 500 thousand dollars.
When we divide them we get the average of a single transaction, which is 33.33 dollars.
Did you see how the raw counter turns into a calculated value that has weight in the business?
And now we go down to the engine room, our kitchen: the ETL and Standardization.
The place where the data is washed and cleaned every 15 minutes.
Look at the mess on the left: scrambled codes from the source.
Like CI and Cash In, or P2P and Transfer.
On the right, after the magic of Standardization, all of this is unified into very clean values.
Like CASH_IN and P2P_TRANSFER.
This unification is what makes the reports come out accurate to the last bit, without any duplication.
And here comes the role of Enrichment, where we apply the financial business rules.
The rule here is called the 60-40 Commission Split.
Meaning the ETL automatically calculates the commission as 60% of the fees, and the remaining 40% is net revenue.
Complex calculations happening in the background without us feeling it.
This journey summarizes the whole ETL Flow.
First, Extract: we pull the data every 15 minutes.
Second, Transform: for cleaning and applying the 60-40 rules we were just talking about.
Third, Load, and this has the most important part of all: the Post-Load Reconciliation.
We must make sure that the totals that left the source are exactly what arrived at the target.
There is no room for error here.
We've reached the peak, the moment in which all this effort crystallizes: the daily Mobile Money report.
Let's see how January 15, 2024 went.
How is this report built?
Seven very simple steps in the Report Designer.
We log in, open the designer, choose the ready cubes, and define what goes in the rows and columns.
We choose our measures, put in the filters, and finally set a schedule so the report is sent automatically at 6 in the morning.
Terrible complexity in the background provides simplicity and comfort for the user.
And this is the final report; imagine the table filling up in front of us row after row.
Cash-In, Cash-Out, and P2P, which recorded the highest transaction count.
Bill Payment, Airtime and Merchant; each row shows the count, value, fees and success rate.
These aren't just numbers; this is the pulse of the business on that day.
This chart gives us the geographic summary: the day's revenues split across the regions.
Central dominates with 40%, then Eastern with 20%, and Western with 18%, and so on.
A quick visual view helps decision makers direct their marketing effort in seconds.
The summary for that day was astonishing: 125,847 transactions, with a total reaching 4.2 million dollars.
Here we must stress a golden rule: the overall average is computed by dividing this total value by the total count.
Don't compute an average of the averages in the table, because that gives a completely misleading number.
We've reached the last and most important station in the data world: Governance and Data Masking.
How do we keep control of this treasure and protect it?
The magic of masking shows up here: on the left the full MSISDN, the mobile number, and the name appears as John Mokasa.
This is very dangerous as personal information, or PII.
But on the right, after masking, the number is masked and only the last four digits are visible, and the name only the first letter.
Immediate privacy protection while keeping the report useful.
And so that we can trust this data, governance imposes very strict conditions to get a trust score of 80% or more.
The conditions are like the data being fresh, with no more than two hours having passed on it.
The amounts must be logical, between 0 and 10 million.
And of course applying top encryption standards like AES-256 for stored data.
And TLS 1.2 plus while it is being transferred: total security.
And in the end, do you think what business secrets and opportunities we could discover when our data pipeline reaches 100% confidence?
Building strong data engineering is not just stacking numbers.
It's building trust, and building a future we can rely on.
Thank you very much for your focus and for following along, and see you in future explainers.
One row per transaction.
